title: The Cataract-Glaucoma-Neuropathy Nexus
summary: A comprehensive guide to the complex interplay between lens pathology and optic nerve dysfunction. Understanding when a cataract masks a sick nerve and how the lens itself can trigger sight-threatening glaucoma.

sections.title: The RAPD Paradox in Cataract
sections.content: A fundamental rule in clinical ophthalmology: Cataract alone—no matter how dense—does NOT cause a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD). Because light is scattered rather than blocked from reaching the retina, the total amount of light reaching the photoreceptors remains sufficient to drive the pupillary reflex. If an RAPD is present in a cataractous eye, you MUST investigate for concurrent optic nerve or extensive retinal disease.

sections.title: Etiology of RAPD in Cataractous Patients
The 'Inverse' RAPD Trick
content: Used when one pupil is fixed (miotic, traumatic, or surgical) but the other is reactive.
Observe the reactive pupil only.
Shine light in the reactive eye: it constricts (direct).
Shine light in the non-reactive/opaque eye: if the reactive pupil dilates, an RAPD is present in the opaque eye.
Critical for pre-operative assessment in dense cataracts with suspected nerve damage.

sections.title: Glaucoma Leading to Cataract
content: Glaukomflecken: Minute white subcapsular opacities from lens epithelial necrosis post-acute angle closure.
Miotics: Long-term Pilocarpine use is associated with anterior subcapsular opacification.
Metabolic: Severe chronic IOP elevation disrupts lens fiber nutrition.
Iatrogenic: Post-Trabeculectomy/Tube surgery (mechanical contact or metabolic change).

sections.title: Red Flags: The Urgent Cataract
content: RAPD in an eye with simple nuclear sclerosis.
IOP > 40 mmHg with an intumescent (swollen) cataract.
Iridescent/polychromatic 'crystals' in the aqueous humor.
Sudden vision loss better than light perception in a mature white cataract.
Asymmetric AC depth between the two eyes.

rows: High C:D ratio, Notch in RIM, arcuate defects.
Pallor out of proportion to cupping.

sections.title: Pre-Op Evaluation of Opaque Media
content: 1. B-Scan Ultrasonography: Rule out RD, tumors, or posterior staphyloma.
2. Potential Acuity Meter (PAM): Estimate post-op VA if media allows.
3. Flash VEP: Assess optic nerve pathway integrity.
4. Entoptic Phenomenon: Patient visualizes retinal vasculature via trans-scleral light.
5. Two-Point Discrimination: Gross test of macular function.

content.explanation: Phacomorphic (Big lens), Phacolytic (Leaky lens), Phacoantigenic (Allergy to lens), Phacotopic (Displaced lens).

sections.title: Surgical Pearls for Phacomorphic Cases
content: Pre-op Hyperosmotics: IV Mannitol 20% (1-2g/kg) to dehydrate the vitreous and deepen the AC.
Trypan Blue: Essential for visualizing the capsule in white cataracts.
Argentinian Flag Sign Prevention: Decompress the lens with a needle aspiration before completing the capsulorhexis.
Healon 5 / OVD: Use high-viscosity cohesives to maintain the chamber and push the iris back.
Large incision ECCE: Consider if the cornea is too edematous for safe Phaco.

sections.title: Recent Advances: The EAGLE Study
sections.content: The Landmark EAGLE Trial (Effectiveness in Angle-closure Glaucoma of Lens Extraction) demonstrated that clear lens extraction showed greater efficacy and was more cost-effective than laser peripheral iridotomy as a first-line treatment for primary angle-closure glaucoma with IOP > 30 mmHg or primary angle-closure. This has shifted the management paradigm toward earlier lens removal in patients with narrow angles and glaucoma risk.

sections.title: Phacolytic Management Protocol
content: 1. Rapid IOP Reduction: Topical Beta-blockers, Alpha-agonists, and Oral Acetazolamide.
2. Inflammation Control: Intensive topical steroids (Pred Forte q1h).
3. Urgent Surgery: Usually within 24-48 hours. The goal is to remove the protein source.
4. Copious AC Washout: Ensure all lens proteins and macrophages are removed from the angle.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: A dense cataract does not cause RAPD, but a RAPD can be caused by the advanced glaucoma the cataract itself triggered.
In phacolytic glaucoma, the angle is OPEN, distinguishing it from phacomorphic.
Pseudoexfoliation (PXF) is the 'Great Masquerader'—causing both weak zonules (cataract surgery risk) and secondary open-angle glaucoma.
Always check the fellow eye: Disc-at-risk suggests NAION; narrow angles suggest Phacomorphic risk.
